Wat la ka rukom synshar ha ki British Areas ha ri India ka dei ka

La buh ha ka Centre ia ki Subjects kum ka Defence, Foreign 
Relations, Railway, Posts bad Telegraphs Currency bad coinage, 
Tariffe bad Customs, Public Debts, Civil bad Criminal Laws and 
procedure. Shipping, Major Ports etc., ki subjects ha kiba donkam 
ban ioh kajuh ka rukom pyniaid ha baroh kawei ka ri India. 

Ki Subjects jong ki Provinces pat ki long kum ka Local self-

Ka 'Residuary power' ne ka bor ban thaw ain ha ki Subjects kiba

Areas' kiba hap hapoh ka jylli trei kam jong ka Shillong 
Municipality bad jong ka Shillong Cantonment. Ha ka Election

Roy u la ioh 358 votes bad u Srijut Sivanath Dutta u la ioh 112 
votes. Nalor ki Elected Members jong ka Legislative Council ki 
don ruh ki 'Nominated Members'.

Ha Ri India ha kito ki por don ar tylli ki rukom S 3 mshar: Kaba

beit da ki Phareng (British Areas). La bynta ia kine ki jaka ha ki

"The meeting of the Khasis held on 25*'’ May 1943 under the 
auspicies of Khasi National Dorbar, learnt with deep concern of 
the rumour that Mr. A.R.H. Macdonald I.C.S., Deputy 
Commissioner and Political Agent Khasi States, Khasi & Jaintia 
Hills is under order of transfer. 

The Khasi people have found in Mr. Macdonald an able and 
competent administrator both as D.C. and P.O. Khasi & Jaintia 
Hills. His handling of the food situation and other measures arising 
out of the war conditions has created confidence and given 
satisfaction. His transfer from this District at this time would be 
most unfortunate. The Meeting therefore, urge upon His Excellency 
to retain Mr. Macdonald as D.C. and P.O. of his District, at least, 
for the duration of the war".

U V.P. Menon, Secretary jong ka Sorkar India, Ministry of 
States ha ka kot jong u, 'The Story of the Integration of the 
Indian States', u ong - 

"THE KHASI HILL STATES , a tribal area in Assam, were 
twenty-five in number. The chiefs of these States, known as 
Siems, were generally elected by the people: a number of them 
were Christians. Before the transfer of power, the Crown 
Representative's relations with these Staes were conducted 
through the Governor of Assam. These States did not accede 
to India on 15*'’ August 1947. the old practice continued, by 
which the Government of Assam administered these areas 
on behalf of the Government of India under the Indian 
(Foreign Jurisdiction Order in Council). Later in the year 
these States, which had meanwhile formed a federation of 
their own, executed an Agreement continuing in force, with 
certain exceptions, existing administrative arrangements with 
the Dominion of India and the Province of Assam. Thereafter, 
the rulers individually and collectively acceded to the Indian 
Union. The Instrument of Accession, subject to the provision 
of the Agreement, empowered the Dominion Legislature to 
make laws for the Khasi Hill State in respect of any matter. 

The future of these States under the new Constitution was 
the subject of prolonged discussion between the States 
Ministry and the the Siems and their advisers, the Reverend 
Nichols-Roy being their chief spokesman. The people in the 
States wished to preserve their tradition and customs as far 
as possible. They were anxious to maintain their autonomy, 
and were opposed to the idea of outright merger with Assam. 
The Government of India ultimately deaded that the district 
councils in the tribal areas should be given a large measure 
of autonomy. Detailed and specific provisions for the 
governance of the Khasi Hill States and odier tribal areas of

Assam were included in the Sixth Schedule to the Indian 
Constitution".*

have difiierent tradition^ culture and civilization of their own. From 
time inunemorial ttiey had their indigenous demoor^c rulers called

But we find that the Sixth Schedule does not provide adequate 
safeguards for all those rights, privileges and decrocratic 
institutions. The Consitution Making Duihar of the Khasi States 
as far back as 1940 had foreseen this and demanded a separate 
schedule for the whole District of Khasi Jaintia Hills. 

The purpose of the embodiment of the Sixth Schedule in the 
Constitution is that the Tribal people should decide for themselves 
and not to have things decided for them. But the introduction of 
arbitrary nominations to the District Council is foreign to the 
democratic traditions of the Khasis and at the same time defeats 
that very purpose. 

As a protest against this innovation which is a challenge to the 
feelings of the Khasis, after unsuccessful attempts to obtain redress 
from die Government of Assam, a procession headed by students 
was taken out on the 27* June 1952, the day of inauguration of 
the District Council. The procession was peaceful one and free of 
all intentions of causing breach of public peace. The Government 
of Assam met the procession by a well-prepared force of armed 
police who engaged the demonstrators with tear-gas and lathi 
charge, a fact which gave rise to a just resentment of the Khasis.

Fourty three of the demonstrators were arrested while public 
resentment was cooled down by interference of Khasi leaders who 
love and work for peace. Strangely enough, a few minutes after 
the above incident the procession was allowed to reform itself and 
to proceed, this time with a much large crowd through the main 
roads of Shillong which were previously prohibited areas. Thus 
the 'right of expression' of the Khasis was cut and their feelings of 
insecurity aggravated. 

In addition to the imposition of nomintation to the District Council 
the existence of the following provisions, among others, have served 
to increase the sense of insecurity and fears of the Khasis :- 

1. That assent to the laws passed by the District Council will be 
given by the Govenor not acting in his discreation. 

2. The exclusion of Shillong for all practical purposes from the 
jurisdiction of the District Council. 

3. That licences and leases for the purpose of prospecting for.

and the extraction of minerals from our District are to be 
granted by the Assam Government. 

4. That large portion of the income derived from the District has 
to be shared with the State Government. 

The partition of India has extensively hard hit the Southern portion 
of Khasi Hills. People in that area were and used to be prosperous

and rich. The partition brought cessation of trade with Sylhet bad 
East Bengal and the once valuable and wealth producing 
commodities became useless and unusable with the consequence 
that these people were reduced to dire poverty. The attempt to air- 
lift the produce last year could only transport a microscopic portion 
of it. The area does not produce life-maintaining commodities and 
the people are suffering from want and starvation. Driven by 
hunger a nuber of our kith and kin (more than 1000) was reported 
to have separated from us and migrated to Pakistan. This is heart- 
paining to us as a people and likely a danger to the State. The 
proposed attempt of the Assam Government to supply rice to those 
people at control rate will be of no value because they have no 
more purchasing power. Their condition is no better than those of 
refugees. 

We opposed the proposal of making Assamese the State language 
of Assam. As Hill Tribes we are having to learn besides our own 
vernacular, English and Hindi which is athe lingua franca of India; 
addition of Assamese over and above these will be very heavy to 
our boys and girls in schools and colleges. 

The Hills of Assam are contiguous and the people inhabiting them 
are more or less of the same stock, having affinity of culture, ways 
of life, character and in many other respects. They have common 
understanding, common fear of encroachment and exploitation 
by major communities. The unification of these hills under one 
administration and tmder the Indiem Union will, it is hoped, meet 
the aspirations of all the Tribal people.
